source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2
notes_on_source: Verse 30 is missing from the source (jumps from v29 to v31).

verses.translation: And then there came{H935} to Yeshua certain Separatists{H6504} and wise-men of the old religion{H1881} who had come from Yerushalayim{H3389}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פרושים (perushim — 'Separatists/those who separate', from פרש H6504 — 'to separate/distinguish'). This is the HEBREW meaning of the word: those who separate themselves for purity. Greek has Φαρισαῖοι (Pharisaioi) — a transliteration of the Hebrew. A back-translator from Greek would simply re-transliterate back. The Hebrew preserves the original etymological meaning: they are 'the separated ones.'

Uses חכמי הדת ישנה (chakhmei ha-dat yeshanah — 'wise-men of the old religion/law'). Greek has γραμματεῖς (grammateis — 'scribes/writers'). A back-translator from 'scribes' would use סופרים (sofrim — 'scribes/writers'). The Hebrew term is entirely different: these are not mere writers/copyists but 'sages of the ancient tradition.' The word דת (dat, H1881) is the Aramaic/later Hebrew word for law/religion (Ezra 7:26, Esther 1:8,13,15,19, 3:8). The qualifier ישנה ('old/ancient') distinguishes this tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Separatists' (פרושים — etymological meaning). Greek: 'Pharisees' (Φαρισαῖοι — transliteration).
Hebrew: 'wise-men of the old religion' (חכמי הדת ישנה). Greek: 'scribes' (γραμματεῖς). Entirely different titles.
translation_notes: 'Separatists' for perushim preserves the Hebrew etymological meaning.
'Old religion' for dat yeshanah — דת is specifically the law/decree/religion, not merely 'tradition.' The qualifier 'old' distinguishes it.

verses.translation: And when they saw{H7200} some of his disciples eating{H398} without ritual hand-washing, they despised{H959} them.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נטילת ידים (netilat yadayim — 'ritual hand-washing'). This is the specific RABBINIC HALAKHIC term for the ritual of hand-washing before meals — a technical term from Rabbinic Judaism that appears in the Mishnah (Yadayim, Berakhot) and Talmud. Greek has κοιναῖς χερσίν, τοῦτ᾿ ἔστιν ἀνίπτοις ('with common/defiled hands, that is, unwashed'). A back-translator from Greek would write בידים טמאות ('with impure hands') or בידים בלתי רחוצות ('with unwashed hands'). The Hebrew uses the precise halakhic technical term that only a Hebrew author immersed in Rabbinic practice would employ.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: נטילת ידים (precise halakhic term for ritual hand-washing). Greek: 'common/unwashed hands' (κοιναῖς χερσίν, ἀνίπτοις). The Hebrew has a single technical term; the Greek requires explanation.
translation_notes: 'Ritual hand-washing' for netilat yadayim — this is not merely washing dirty hands but a specific ritual purification act with prescribed amounts of water and methods.

verses.translation: For the Yehudim do not eat{H398} unless they always{H8548} perform ritual hand-washing, according to the decree{H1504} of the ancients{H3453}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses גזירת הישישים (gezirat ha-yeshishim — 'decree of the ancients/elders'). גזירה (gezirah, from גזר H1504 — 'to cut/decree') is the specific RABBINIC term for a rabbinical decree or enacted prohibition — as opposed to a Torah commandment. It implies a legally binding ruling issued by rabbinic authorities. Greek has τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ('the tradition of the elders'). A back-translator from Greek would use מסורת הזקנים (masoret ha-zqenim — 'tradition of the elders'). The Hebrew distinguishes: a גזירה is a DECREE (legislative act); a מסורת is a TRADITION (handed-down custom). The Hebrew says these are not traditions but legally enacted decrees.

Uses הישישים (ha-yeshishim, H3453 — 'the ancients'). This is a different word from זקנים (zqenim — 'elders'). ישישים implies extreme antiquity and age (Job 12:12, 15:10, 29:8, 32:6). Greek πρεσβυτέρων ('elders') would normally back-translate as זקנים. The Hebrew author uses the rarer, more ancient-sounding term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'decree of the ancients' (גזירה — enacted law; ישישים — the very ancient). Greek: 'tradition of the elders' (παράδοσις — handed-down custom; πρεσβυτέρων — elders). Different legal categories.
translation_notes: 'Decree' for gezirah — this is a rabbinic legal ruling, not merely a custom. The distinction matters: Yeshua is challenging not informal traditions but formally enacted rabbinic legislation.
'Ancients' for yeshishim — older and more authoritative than merely 'elders.'

verses.translation: And many{H7227} other statutes{H2706} they were commanded{H6680} to keep{H8104}: this is the ritual washing of their garments{H3682} and silver{H3701} drinking-vessels.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חקים (chuqim, H2706 — 'statutes/enactments'). This is the specific OT word for God's statutes (Lev 18:4, Deut 4:1, 6:1). Greek has no equivalent here (the verse structure differs). The Hebrew ironically applies the Torah's word for divine statutes to human ritual regulations — the very confusion Yeshua will challenge.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'statutes' (חקים — Torah's word for God's laws). Greek: various (the verse structure in Greek differs considerably, with more detail about washing of cups, pots, and brazen vessels).

verses.translation: And because of this the Separatists{H6504} asked{H7592} Yeshua, saying{H559}: Why do your disciples not keep{H8104} the decrees{H1504} of the ancestral{H1} ancients{H3453}, but eat{H398} bread{H3899} all day with hands not ritually washed?

one_way_hebrew: Uses גזירות ישישי האבות (gezirot yeshishei ha-avot — 'decrees of the ancients of the fathers'). This triple-layered authority designation (decree + ancients + patriarchs) is a distinctly Hebrew/Rabbinic authority chain. Greek has τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ('the tradition of the elders'). The Hebrew is far more elaborate in its institutional terminology.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'decrees of the ancients of the fathers' (triple authority chain). Greek: 'tradition of the elders' (single term).
Hebrew: 'eat bread all the day' (פת כל הים). Greek has no time reference. Hebrew adds the habitual 'all day' detail.

verses.translation: And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559} to them: Well did the prophet{H5030} Yeshayahu{H3470} prophesy{H5012} of you deceivers{H7411}, saying: This people{H5971} honors{H3513} me with speech{H1697}, but their heart{H3820} is far{H7350} from me.

one_way_hebrew: ISAIAH QUOTATION: Hebrew quotes Isaiah 29:13 — 'this people honors me with speech, but their heart is far from me' (העם הזה...בפיו ובשפתיו כבדוני ולבו רחק ממני). The Hebrew preserves the Isaiah source with minor variations. Greek quotes the LXX version of Isaiah. The Hebrew retains the MT form.

Uses רמאים (rama'im — 'deceivers/fraudsters', from רמה H7411 — 'to beguile/deceive'). Greek has ὑποκριταί ('hypocrites' — actors). A back-translator from Greek would use צבועים (tsevu'im — 'hypocrites/painted ones'). The Hebrew says the Pharisees are not merely play-actors (Greek concept) but DECEIVERS — active fraudsters. The OT roots of רמה include Jacob deceiving Esau (Gen 29:25) and Delilah deceiving Samson (Judg 16:10,13).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'deceivers' (רמאים — active fraud). Greek: 'hypocrites' (ὑποκριταί — theatrical pretense). Different moral characterizations.
Hebrew: 'honors me with speech' (מדבר — words). Greek: 'honors me with their lips' (τοῖς χείλεσίν). Different body part.
translation_notes: 'Deceivers' for rama'im — stronger than 'hypocrites.' These are not merely actors but deliberate fraudsters.
textual_notes: Isaiah 29:13 (MT): 'Because this people draws near with their mouth and with their lips they honor me, but their heart is far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men learned by rote.' The Hebrew Mark preserves the MT; Greek uses the LXX.

verses.translation: In vain{H2600} they honor{H3513} me, teaching{H3925} the instructions{H4148} and commandments{H4687} of men{H376}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוסרים (musarim — 'instructions/disciplines', plural of מוסר H4148). Again the Proverbs wisdom-tradition term. These are not merely 'doctrines' (Greek διδασκαλίας) but wisdom-tradition 'instructions' — the word implies the entire apparatus of Rabbinic moral discipline. A back-translator from Greek would use הוראות (hora'ot — 'teachings/doctrines').

verses.translation: And you forsake{H5800} the commandments{H4687} of God{H430} and seize{H8610} what has been transmitted by men{H376}. And there come to them cups{H1375} and silver{H3701} drinking-vessels and similar many{H7227} things{H1697}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גביעים (gevi'im — 'cups/goblets', H1375). This is the specific OT word for Joseph's silver divination cup (Gen 44:2,12,16,17). Greek has no equivalent here (the verse structure differs). The Hebrew author uses the Genesis-Joseph cup vocabulary for the ritual washing vessels.

verses.translation: And likewise he said{H559} to them: You break{H7665} the commandments{H4687} of HaShem{H8034} in order to keep{H8104} your customs{H4941}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שוברים (shovrim — 'breaking', from שבר H7665 — 'to shatter/break'). This is the word for breaking a vessel, a covenant, or a law violently (Ex 32:19 Moses broke the tablets; Jer 19:10 breaking the potter's flask). Greek has ἀθετεῖτε ('you set aside/nullify'). A back-translator from 'set aside' would use מבטלים (mevatlin — 'annulling'). The Hebrew says they SHATTER God's commandments — the violence of Moses smashing the tablets.
Again uses השם (HaShem — 'the Name') for God. Consistent with Hebrew authorship.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'break/shatter' (שבר — violent destruction). Greek: 'set aside/reject' (ἀθετέω — nullification). Different intensity.

verses.translation: As Moshe{H4872} said{H559}: Honor{H3513} your father{H1} and your mother{H517}; and whoever curses{H7043} his father or his mother shall surely die{H4191}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM TORAH QUOTATION: כבד את אביך ואת אמך (Exodus 20:12 / Deuteronomy 5:16) and אשר יקלל אביו ואמו מות יומת (Exodus 21:17 / Leviticus 20:9). The Hebrew preserves the EXACT MT wording including the emphatic Hebrew infinitive absolute construction מות יומת ('dying he shall die' — 'shall surely die'). Greek renders this as θανάτῳ τελευτάτω ('let him die the death') — a close but not exact rendering. A back-translator from Greek would not independently reproduce the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction.
translation_notes: מות יומת (mot yumat — 'surely die') — the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction that intensifies the verb. This exact form appears 47 times in the Torah as the penalty formula.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:12 and 21:17 — Yeshua quotes Torah to challenge the Pharisees' oral law, using the exact Hebrew text.

verses.translation: But you say{H559}: When any man{H120} vows{H5087} a vow{H5088} on behalf of his father{H1} and mother{H517}, that it might benefit them —

one_way_hebrew: Uses נדר (neder, H5088 — 'vow'). This is the OT vow system (Num 30:3-16, Deut 23:22-24). The Hebrew discusses the corban/vow system using native vocabulary. Greek has Κορβᾶν (Korban — a Hebrew loanword transliterated into Greek), then explains ὅ ἐστιν δῶρον ('which is, a gift'). The Greek needs to explain the Hebrew term to its audience; the Hebrew uses it naturally.
greek_deviations: Greek explains Korban as a foreign term that needs translation. Hebrew uses the vow system naturally without explanation — suggesting Hebrew priority.

verses.translation: And afterward you do not allow{H5117} him to fulfill{H7999} his duty to father{H1} and mother{H517}.
Thus you break{H7665} the commandments{H4687} of HaShem{H8034} for the sake of your customs{H4941} that you have devised{H4672}. And many{H7227} other evil{H7451} things you do{H6213}.
And then he called{H7121} the people{H5971} and said{H559} to them: Hear{H8085} me and understand{H995} me.

one_way_hebrew: שמעוני ותבינוני ('hear me and understand me') echoes the Shema pattern and the wisdom call. שמע + בין together appear in Deuteronomy 9:1 ('Hear, O Israel') and Proverbs 1:2 ('to know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of understanding'). The dual imperative form is characteristically Hebrew.

verses.translation: Nothing{H1697} from outside{H2351} entering{H935} a man{H120} is able{H3201} to defile{H2930} him; but what goes out{H3318} from the heart{H3820} of a man{H120} defiles{H2930} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses two different words for 'defile': לטנפו (letanfo — 'to dirty/soil him') and מלכלכו (melakhlekho — 'to defile/dirty him'). The first (טנף) is a practical term for physical soiling; the second (לכלך) is specifically moral defilement. Greek uses κοινόω ('to make common/profane') for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word twice, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes between external contamination and internal defilement.
greek_deviations: Hebrew uses two different defilement words (טנף and לכלך). Greek uses one (κοινόω) for both.

verses.translation: Whoever has ears{H241} to hear{H8085}, let him hear{H8085}.

textual_notes: This formula echoes Deuteronomy 29:3 ('YHWH has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear') and Ezekiel 12:2 ('who have eyes to see but do not see, ears to hear but do not hear').

verses.translation: And when Yeshua entered{H935} a house{H1004}, the disciples asked{H7592} him what that parable meant to say{H559}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses התמונה (ha-temunah — 'the image/figure/likeness'). In the OT, תמונה (H8544) is the word for the form/likeness of God (Num 12:8 'the form (תמונת) of YHWH he beholds'; Deut 4:12,15,16). Greek has παραβολή ('parable'). A back-translator from 'parable' would use משל (mashal — 'parable/proverb'), not the theophany-word תמונה. The Hebrew says the disciples asked about 'the image/vision' — framing Yeshua's teaching as a divine revelation rather than a story.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'image/figure' (תמונה — theophanic term). Greek: 'parable' (παραβολή — teaching story). Different framing.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: Are you then also fools{H6612} who do not understand{H995}? Do you not understand that nothing that enters{H935} the body{H1320} of a man{H120} is able{H3201} to defile{H2930} him?

one_way_hebrew: Uses פתאים (peta'im, H6612 — 'fools/simpletons'). This is the Proverbs wisdom-tradition term for the naive/gullible (Prov 1:4,22,32, 7:7, 8:5, 9:4,6, 14:15, 22:3). Greek has ἀσύνετοι ('without understanding'). A back-translator from Greek would use חסרי בינה ('lacking understanding'). The Hebrew uses the specific Solomonic wisdom category.

verses.translation: For it does not enter{H935} the body but only the belly{H990}, and goes out{H3318} through nature, cleansing{H5352}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα ('purifying all foods') — a parenthetical remark often interpreted as declaring all foods clean. The Hebrew has simply מנקה ('cleansing') without this editorial expansion.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: The evil{H7451} things{H1697} that stir{H5128} from the heart{H3820} from within — they are what defile.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מתנועעים (mitno'a'im — 'stirring/shaking', from נוע H5128 — 'to shake/waver'). This is the verb used for the earth shaking (Isa 24:20), trees swaying (Isa 7:2), and wandering/vagrancy (Gen 4:12 Cain's sentence). Greek has ἐκπορεύεται ('goes out'). A back-translator would use יוצאים (yotzim — 'going out'). The Hebrew describes evil as stirring/shaking within the heart before erupting — a more vivid and dynamic image.

verses.translation: Evil{H7451} thoughts{H4284} and adulteries{H5003} and murders{H7523} and thefts{H1589}.

one_way_hebrew: The vice list uses OT/Torah vocabulary: ניאופים (ni'ufim — 'adulteries', from נאף H5003, the Seventh Commandment); רציחות (retzichot — 'murders', from רצח H7523, the Sixth Commandment); גניבות (genevot — 'thefts', from גנב H1589, the Eighth Commandment). These are the exact verb roots of the Ten Commandments. The Hebrew author catalogs sins using Decalogue vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list has 4 items. Greek list has 6 items (adds πορνεῖαι — 'fornications' and πλεονεξίαι — 'covetings'). Hebrew is more concise.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:13-15 (MT): 'You shall not murder (לא תרצח). You shall not commit adultery (לא תנאף). You shall not steal (לא תגנב).' The vice list follows the Decalogue order.

verses.translation: Miserliness{H3596}, lust{H2530}, pride{H1346}, foolishness{H5531}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סכלות (sikhlut, H5531 — 'foolishness'). This is the Ecclesiastes/Proverbs wisdom-tradition term (Eccl 1:17, 2:3,12,13, 7:25, 10:1,13). Greek has ἀφροσύνη ('lack of sense'). A back-translator would use אולת or חסרון דעת, not the specific Qohelet term.
Uses כילאות (kila'ut — 'miserliness/stinginess'). This is a distinctly Hebrew term for hoarding/withholding. Greek has πονηρίαι ('wickedness') or similar. Different vice categories.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has 4 items. Greek has 7 items (adds βλασφημία — 'blasphemy', ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός — 'evil eye', ὑπερηφανία — 'arrogance'). Different vice lists.

verses.translation: All{H3605} these evils{H7451} stir{H5128} from the heart{H3820}, and these defile{H2930} a man{H120}.

textual_notes: Genesis 6:5: 'YHWH saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.' Yeshua's teaching echoes the Genesis diagnosis of the human heart.

verses.translation: And Yeshua arose{H6965} and went{H1980} to the regions of Tsor{H6865} and Tsidon{H6721}, and entered{H935} one house{H1004} and did not wish{H7521} that anyone know{H3045} him; yet he was not able{H3201} to be hidden{H5641}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אבה (avah, H14 — 'wished/consented'). This is a specifically Hebrew verb for willingness/consent that appears throughout the OT (Gen 24:5,8, Deut 2:30, 10:10, 25:7, Judg 19:25, 1 Sam 22:17, 26:23, 31:4). Greek has ἤθελεν ('wished'). While the meanings overlap, אבה is a verb with no exact Greek equivalent — it implies deep, considered consent/willingness.

verses.translation: For a certain woman{H802} who had a daughter{H1323} who was satan-possessed came{H935} to him and bowed{H3766} at his feet{H7272}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'satan-possessed' (מושטנת). Greek: 'had an unclean spirit' (πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον). The שטן vs. δαιμόνιον pattern continues.

verses.translation: And she was a fine woman from the family of Syria, and she begged{H1245} him to drive out{H1644} the satan{H7854} from her daughter{H1323}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says she was 'from the family of Syria' (ממשפחת סוריא). Greek says she was Ἑλληνίς, Συροφοινίκισσα τῷ γένει ('a Greek, a Syro-Phoenician by birth'). The Hebrew does not call her 'Greek' at all — only Syrian. A back-translator from Greek would include the 'Greek' designation. The Hebrew identifies her by clan/family (משפחה, H4940 — the OT kinship unit, Josh 7:14, Judg 6:15) rather than by ethnicity/nationality.
Hebrew also adds that she was נאה (na'eh — 'fine/beautiful'). This detail is absent from Greek. The Hebrew author notes her appearance — an eyewitness-type detail.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'fine woman from the family of Syria.' Greek: 'Greek woman, Syro-Phoenician by birth.' Different ethnic identification.
Hebrew adds 'fine/beautiful' (נאה). Greek has no appearance detail.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559}: First{H7223} a man{H120} is obligated to help{H5826} his children{H1121}, for it is not a good{H2896} thing{H1697} to take{H3947} the bread{H3899} from the children{H1121} in order to give{H5414} it to dogs{H3611}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew frames the saying with חייב (chayyav — 'obligated'). This is a HALAKHIC term — a legal obligation. The Hebrew says it is legally obligatory to feed one's children first. Greek has ἄφες πρῶτον χορτασθῆναι τὰ τέκνα ('let the children first be satisfied'). The Hebrew frames this as Torah-obligation; the Greek frames it as sequence.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a man is OBLIGATED to help his children' (legal duty). Greek: 'let the children first be satisfied' (priority of sequence).

verses.translation: And she answered{H6030}: Truth{H571} it is, my lord{H113}; yet the whelps{H1484} of the dogs{H3611} eat{H398} the crumbs{H6595} of bread{H3899} that fall{H5307} beneath{H8478} the table{H7979} of the masters{H113}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גורי הכלבים (gurei ha-kelavim — 'the whelps/puppies of the dogs'). The word גור (gur, H1484) is the OT word for a young animal/whelp — used of lion cubs (Gen 49:9, Deut 33:22, Nah 2:12). Greek has κυνάρια ('little dogs/puppies'). A back-translator from Greek would use כלבים קטנים ('little dogs'), not the literary/zoological term גור. The Hebrew word choice gives the woman's response a more dignified, literary quality.

Uses האדונים (ha-adonim — 'the masters/lords', plural of אדון H113). This is the word used for God (אדני — 'my Lord') and for human masters. Greek has κυρίων ('lords'). The Hebrew woman addresses Yeshua as אדון and speaks of 'the masters' — the double use of the same root creates a theological echo: the crumbs from THE Master's table.
translation_notes: 'Whelps' for gurei — preserving the OT zoological term rather than the diminutive 'puppies.'

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to her: For this word{H1697}, your daughter{H1323} shall be healed{H7495}. Behold, the satan{H7854} has gone out{H3318} from her.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says 'for this word' (בעד דבר זה) your daughter shall be healed. Greek says 'for this saying' (διὰ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον). Similar meaning, but the Hebrew uses דבר (davar) which means both 'word' and 'thing/matter' — the woman's WORD becomes the THING that heals. This double meaning only works in Hebrew.
Hebrew says 'shall be healed' (תתרפא). Greek says 'the demon has gone out' (ἐξελήλυθεν τὸ δαιμόνιον). The Hebrew focuses on healing; the Greek on exorcism. Different priorities.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your daughter shall be healed' (healing focus). Greek: 'the demon has gone out' (exorcism focus).
Hebrew: 'the satan' (השטן). Greek: 'the demon' (τὸ δαιμόνιον). שטן vs. δαιμόνιον again.

verses.translation: And then he went out{H3318} from the regions of Tsor{H6865}, passing through Tsidon{H6721}, and came{H935} to the sea{H3220} of the Galil{H1551} toward Decapolis.

translation_notes: דכפוליס (Decapolis) — a Greek loanword preserved in brackets in the source, indicating the Hebrew author recognized it as a foreign term.

verses.translation: And they brought{H935} to him one{H259} man{H376} deaf{H2795} and mute, begging{H1245} him in prayer{H8605} that he lay{H7760} his hand{H3027} upon him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חרש ואלם (cheresh ve-ilem — 'deaf and mute'). The word חרש (cheresh, H2795) appears in Isaiah 29:18 ('the deaf shall hear the words of a book') and 35:5 ('the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped'). Greek has κωφόν καὶ μογιλάλον ('deaf and speech-impaired'). The Greek μογιλάλος appears only here in the NT and is likely a direct reference to Isaiah 35:6 LXX. Both traditions point to Isaiah, but the Hebrew uses the standard OT vocabulary.
Uses בתפלה (be-tefilah — 'in prayer', H8605). They brought the man 'in prayer' — the request was made as a prayer. Greek has no equivalent.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: they asked 'in prayer' (בתפלה). Greek: they 'begged' (παρακαλοῦσιν). Different register.
textual_notes: Isaiah 35:5-6: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf (חרשים) shall be unstopped... and the tongue of the mute (אלם) shall sing for joy.' This healing fulfills Isaiah's messianic prophecy.

verses.translation: And Yeshua led{H1980} him aside from the inhabited place{H3427}, and put{H7760} his fingers{H676} in his ear{H241}, and spat{H7556} and touched{H5060} his tongue{H3956}.
And looking{H5027} up to the heavens{H8064}, he groaned{H584} and said{H559}: Ephphatha — which means: Be opened{H6605}.

one_way_hebrew: The Hebrew glosses אפתח (Ephphatha — an Aramaic imperative) as פתחו (pitchu — 'be opened', from פתח H6605). The Hebrew author explains an Aramaic word in Hebrew — the same authorial practice seen in Mark 5:41. A translator working from Greek would not need to provide a Hebrew gloss of an Aramaic word already explained in Greek.

Uses מתאנח (mit'anech — 'groaning/sighing', from אנח H584). This is the specific OT word for sighing in distress and compassion (Isa 24:7, Lam 1:4,8, Ezek 9:4, 21:11). The groaning expresses visceral empathy.

verses.translation: And immediately his ears{H241} were opened{H6605}, and the confusion of his tongue{H3956} was loosed{H5425}, and he spoke{H1696} freely.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בלבול לשונו (bilbul leshono — 'the confusion of his tongue'). בלבול means 'confusion/mixing' — related to בבל (Babel, 'confusion', Gen 11:9). Greek has ὁ δεσμὸς τῆς γλώσσης ('the bond of the tongue'). A back-translator from 'bond' would use מוסר (moser — 'bond/chain') or קשר (qesher — 'knot'), not 'confusion.' The Hebrew says the tongue's CONFUSION (Babel) was loosed — an un-Babeling, a reversal of linguistic curse.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'confusion of the tongue' (בלבול — Babel/confusion). Greek: 'bond of the tongue' (δεσμός — chain/binding). Different metaphors.
textual_notes: The healing reverses the Babel curse (Gen 11:7-9) — the tongue's confusion is unbound. This is anti-Babel.

verses.translation: And Yeshua commanded{H6680} him that he not tell{H5046} it to any man{H120}; yet the more he commanded{H6680}, the more they proclaimed{H1540}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגלה (megaleh — 'revealed/uncovered', from גלה H1540 — 'to uncover/reveal/exile'). This is the word for divine revelation (Amos 3:7 'YHWH does nothing without revealing (גלה) his secret to his servants the prophets'). Greek has μᾶλλον περισσότερον ἐκήρυσσον ('they proclaimed it even more'). A back-translator would use הכריזו (hikhirzu — 'proclaimed'). The Hebrew says the people REVEALED — using the prophetic revelation verb.

verses.translation: And they marveled{H8539}, saying{H559}: All{H3605} that Yeshua did{H6213}, he did{H6213} well{H3190}, for he made{H6213} the mute{H483} speak{H1696} and the deaf{H2795} hear{H8085}.

one_way_hebrew: ISAIAH FULFILLMENT: 'He made the mute speak and the deaf hear' — echoing Isaiah 35:5-6 ('the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped... the tongue of the mute shall sing for joy'). The crowd's testimony is framed in Isaiah's messianic vocabulary. The Hebrew preserves the OT source; the Greek translates it.
textual_notes: Isaiah 35:5-6: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf (חרשים) unstopped; then shall the lame leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute (אלם) sing for joy.' The crowd recognizes the Isaiah fulfillment.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 7 in Hebrew is saturated with Rabbinic halakhic terminology that no back-translator from Greek would independently produce. The strongest one-way markers: (1) נטילת ידים ('ritual hand-washing') — the precise Rabbinic technical term from Mishnah Yadayim, where Greek requires explanation ('common/unwashed hands'); (2) גזירת הישישים ('decree of the ancients') — a rabbinic legal category (gezirah = enacted decree), not mere 'tradition'; (3) חכמי הדת ישנה ('wise-men of the old religion') for 'scribes'; (4) רמאים ('deceivers') for 'hypocrites' — different moral category; (5) Two different defilement words (טנף and לכלך) where Greek uses one (κοινόω); (6) תמונה ('image/theophanic form') for 'parable'; (7) בלבול לשונו ('confusion of the tongue' — Babel reversal) for 'bond of the tongue'; (8) Verbatim Torah quotes (Ex 20:12, 21:17) with Hebrew infinitive absolute מות יומת; (9) Decalogue-ordered vice list (adultery, murder, theft); (10) Isaiah 29:13 quoted from MT rather than LXX. The chapter reveals an author thinking entirely within Rabbinic legal categories and Torah vocabulary — the debate over purity law is conducted in Hebrew halakhic language that Greek can only approximate.
